title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident shows AI being used as a tool for impersonation fraud, not a failure of a deployed AI product in the conventional sense. Scammers used deepfake generation to fabricate a convincing interview featuring two real, named public figures, then embedded that fabricated content in fake news articles, reviews, and advertisements to lend credibility to an unlicensed investment platform. The failure is not in a single system making an error but in generative AI capabilities being applied deliberately outside any sanctioned deployment, with no human check in the publication chain capable of catching synthetic content before it reached consumers.

The scale reported by the regulator, a 182 percent increase in removed scams in a single year, indicates that the underlying generation tools are accessible enough to support large, coordinated operations. The elaborate supporting infrastructure, fake articles, positive reviews, and advertisements, means detection requires verifying multiple independent signals rather than spotting a single anomaly. Catching this kind of fraud at the content level would require either platform-side detection of synthetic media before publication or licensing checks attached to financial promotions, neither of which operated here.

What is not established is who created or operated these specific deepfakes, what AI systems were used to generate them, or whether any platform knowingly hosted the content. ASIC's figures are regulatory reports, not legal findings, and no individual or company has been charged in connection with the Boulder Sparhaven material described.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article recently circulated featuring Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock in a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler about an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform called Boulder Sparhaven. The interview never actually happened. This type of scam, which uses artificial intelligence to create convincing deepfake content featuring well-known Australians, is rapidly increasing. The corporate regulator ASIC removed 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase, with fake investment platforms rising 151 percent and phishing scams jumping 279 percent.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is the most commonly impersonated public figure, followed by other politicians and prominent financial figures including Alan Kohler, Tom Piotrowski, and billionaires Dick Smith and Gina Rinehart. Scammers create elaborate webs of deception using fake news articles, positive reviews, and advertisements to build credibility before targeting consumers. ASIC advises people to verify Australian Financial Services licenses through their free public register and check that website information matches official records before investing. Alan Kohler has called for heavy fines against platforms hosting this content and the AI models that generate it.
